analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **ISRS consensus technical guideline** built on a PRISMA review of PubMed 2009-2020 (**81 papers**, 57 single-institution) plus 7 international guidelines. A 10-question survey of **14 committee members** reached strong consensus on only 5 questions.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Geometric tolerance ≤1 mm** on system-specific end-to-end tests, **dosimetric accuracy within 5%**, MLC no wider than 5 mm. Clinical dose for 1 cm lesions ranges **18 to 25 Gy**, lower near eloquent brain; imaging-to-beam-on delay preferably under 5 minutes for mask treatments without real-time monitoring.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Defers QA tolerances to **AAPM TG142, TG198 and TG178** and small-field dosimetry to **IAEA TRS 483** rather than restating them. Its clinical margin claims rest on one small randomized 1 vs 3 mm comparison and retrospective series, including Sneed et al on GK.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents SRS to brain metastases ≤1 cm on Gamma Knife, CyberKnife or SRS-adapted LINACs. Does not represent larger lesions, platform commissioning, or cumulative dose after repeat SRS to the same lesion.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The ≤7-day MRI recommendation is tighter than the **<14 vs ≥14 day** split the cited retrospective series tested. The margin-risk modeling study cited included only 1 of 15 lesions under 1 cm.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The document sets a technical floor for taking sub-cm targets to modern LINACs rather than resolving the margin question, which it calls **the biggest and most controversial variable**. Margin advice stays platform-dependent with no fixed number.

studies.interpretation:
This is a physics-led technical guideline, and it should be read as one. Its central claim is feasibility: sub-centimeter metastases no longer need a frame-based Gamma Knife or cone-based LINAC, provided the program meets geometric and dosimetric floors. It does not claim, and cannot claim, that any technique produces better control or less necrosis, because almost none of the underlying literature measured that. Of the 81 papers, 57 came from single institutions, and much of the corpus is technical reports and phantom or positioning work. The recommendations are best treated as minimum QA standards for a small-target program, not as an outcome-validated protocol.

The margin section is where a radiation oncologist should spend attention. The volume arithmetic is the strongest argument in the paper: at 0.8 cm, a 1-mm expansion nearly doubles the treated volume, and in multi-lesion plans that extra normal brain compounds through dose interplay. The clinical evidence is thinner than the arithmetic. One randomized comparison (80 metastases in 49 pts, 1 vs 3 mm) found no local control difference and more necrosis with the larger margin, which supports minimizing but says nothing about zero versus 1 mm. The cited modeling of necrosis risk across 0.5 to 3 mm margins drew on a lesion set with only 1 of 15 under 1 cm, so it barely speaks to this population. The authors then concede that for these targets the baseline necrosis risk is low enough (Sneed et al: 1% or less at 1 year for lesions up to 1 cm at ≤20 Gy without margin) that a relative increase may not move absolute risk much. That concession pulls against their own margin concern, and the guideline leaves margins platform-dependent rather than resolving it.

The platform caveat carries more weight than it first appears. The no-margin experience is largely frame-based Gamma Knife. On a single-isocenter LINAC with CBCT and a 6-DoF couch, the cited end-to-end data put spatial uncertainty within 1 mm only for targets within 4 cm of isocenter, rising to 2 mm beyond. A reader planning many small, scattered metastases off one isocenter cannot borrow the frame-based no-margin data for the peripheral lesions; the geometry, not the lesion size, decides whether omitting margin is defensible there. Mask choice matters similarly: a dedicated SRS mask roughly halved median displacement against a conventional thermoplastic mask.

On imaging, the 7-day recommendation is an extrapolation. The retrospective series behind it compared contouring MRI under versus at or beyond 14 days, with 12-month local freedom from progression of 95% and 56%. The separate growth data (median 20% volume growth over a median 8 days) make a shorter window plausible, but no cited study tested 7 days directly.

The survey is the most candid part of the paper. Strong consensus on only 5 of 10 questions among 14 expert members, and none on 3, means the field has not converged on the controversial technical choices. What would change this guidance is prospective outcome data on margin omission for small off-axis targets on single-isocenter LINAC plans, and on cumulative normal-brain dose as pts live longer and receive repeat SRS, a problem the authors flag but leave open.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Margin is the decision this moves: a 1-mm margin on a 0.8-cm sphere takes it from 0.268 to 0.524 cc, and randomized 1 vs 3 mm margins showed equal LC with more radionecrosis at 3 mm. On single-isocenter plans, accuracy holds within 1 mm only inside 4 cm of isocenter.

Cumulative normal-brain dose after repeat SRS
2.5 vs 5 mm MLC for sub-cm targets

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Case-based practice guideline sponsored by the **Radiosurgery Society**, built around two cases (7 NSCLC mets; single 3.5-cm posterior fossa colon met, resected) with narrative evidence review.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **<2 cm: 20-24 Gy/1 fx**; **2-4 cm: 27 Gy/3 fx or 30 Gy/5 fx**; >4 cm surgery first, multifraction if inoperable. PTV **1-2 mm (1 mm when possible)** intact; postop PTV typically 2 mm, SRS within 4 weeks.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Anchored on RTOG 9508 and the SRS-alone trials (incl. N107C/RTOG 1270 postop) for 1 to 4 mets; extends **suitability to 1-15 lesions** on observational data and an abstract-only trial. Defers to ASTRO and ASCO-SNO-ASTRO guidance on dose and SRS deferral.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adults with brain metastases, intact or resected, being considered for LINAC or Gamma Knife SRS. Does not represent classical leptomeningeal disease or lesions >6 cm.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Several extensions (nodular LMD SRS in **16 pts**, SCLC SRS, preop SRS LMD benefit) rest on small or non-randomized series. Concurrent-systemic survival data are retrospective and open to confounding by fitness.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The practical shift is toward **volume and V12** as the gate for single vs multifraction SRS and for SRS vs WBRT. Preop SRS is framed as promising but under prospective test, not a default.

studies.interpretation:
The useful move in this guideline is shifting the SRS eligibility conversation from lesion count toward volume and dose. Its suitability table extends the suitable range to 1-15 lesions, well past the 1 to 4 metastases on which RTOG 9508 and the SRS-alone trials, including N107C/RTOG 1270 in the postoperative bed, built the current standard. The authors are open that this extension sits on softer ground: a prospective observational comparison of 2 to 4 versus 5 to 10 lesions with total volume under 15 cc, and an MD Anderson trial of SRS versus WBRT in 4 to 15 metastases that closed early and exists only as an abstract. A reader should treat the 15-lesion ceiling as a reasonable practice boundary rather than a tested one. The cited multivariable signal that tumor volume, not lesion number, carried prognostic weight is the more defensible frame for the patient with many small lesions.

The fractionation guidance is where the document is most actionable for a planner. It keeps ASTRO's single-fraction range below 2 cm and names 27 Gy in 3 or 30 Gy in 5 for 2 to 4 cm, but the stronger argument is dosimetric: single-fraction V12 tracks with symptomatic radionecrosis, so the decision to fractionate should follow whether a plan can meet a V12 objective. The pooled comparison supports that framing for 4-14 cc lesions, where multifraction SRS cut radionecrosis from 23.1% to 7.3%. Above 14 cc the radionecrosis difference (11.7% vs 6.5%) did not reach significance and local control was similar, which suggests fractionation alone does not solve the largest lesions and keeps resection first line there.

On margins the guideline takes a clear position, 1 to 2 mm with 1 mm when setup confidence allows, justified by plan data showing low-dose brain volumes doubling from 0 to 1 mm and tripling at 2 mm. Preoperative SRS is presented as promising rather than established: the lower meningeal disease rate (5.8% vs 16% to 21%) comes from initial non-randomized series, and selection of asymptomatic pts who can wait for treatment likely flatters it. The ongoing prospective trials are the real test.

The concurrent-systemic section leans on retrospective series whose survival gap (41.6 vs 21.5 months) is what confounding by fitness would produce. The defensible read is that holding effective systemic therapy for SRS is not supported, not that concurrency improves survival. The named exceptions, BRAF inhibitors with intratumoral bleeding and erlotinib in pts also receiving WBRT, are the ones worth remembering.

As a case-based society document, the source states no evidence grading or panel process, so its recommendations carry the weight of expert synthesis. Where it tracks ASTRO and ASCO-SNO-ASTRO guidance it reinforces current practice; where it extends (15 lesions, nodular LMD, SCLC) it marks a direction, not settled ground.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Single-fraction V12 of 5, 10 and >15 cc maps to ~10%, 15% and 20% symptomatic radionecrosis, and multifraction SRS cut radionecrosis 23.1% to 7.3% in 4-14 cc lesions. PTV 1 mm when setup allows, since 0 to 2 mm triples low-dose brain volume.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Most data support SRS concurrent with systemic therapy without a washout, so holding an active regimen for radiosurgery is not supported. Exceptions flagged: BRAF inhibitors (intratumoral bleeding) and erlotinib in pts also receiving WBRT.

studies.name: Natural History of DCIS of the Breast: A Review
studies.tldr: 14–53% of DCIS misdiagnosed as benign progressed to invasive cancer over 10+ yrs; CS+RT recurrence 8.9% vs 22.5% after CS alone.

studies.significance: Latency is the RT-relevant detail: low-grade DCIS recurs less often early but its recurrence keeps rising with long follow-up, and Page's untreated cases invaded at 23 and 31 yrs. Omission arguments for low-grade DCIS built on short-horizon ipsilateral event rates are reading an incomplete curve.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative review; MEDLINE plus citation search of key reviews. Six evidence streams: misdiagnosed-as-benign follow-up series, recurrence after local therapy, autopsy, risk-factor epidemiology, animal models, mathematical models. **No formal pooling** of progression estimates.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **14–53%** of untreated misdiagnosed DCIS progressed to invasive cancer over 10 or more yrs. Autopsy median DCIS prevalence **8.9%** (range 0–14.7%) vs **1.3%** undiagnosed invasive cancer.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: RT data come from the Boyages meta-analysis comparing CS alone, CS+RT and mastectomy; the RT reduction held across comedo, necrosis and high/intermediate grade subgroups (see table). **No dose, fractionation or boost data** reported.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: NSABP B-17 and EORTC 10853 established RT after BCS for DCIS; this review supplies the natural-history frame, not new efficacy data. It predates RTOG 9804 and the active-surveillance trials (LORIS, COMET, LORD), which test low-risk DCIS management prospectively.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Misdiagnosis series skew low grade, so they say little about high-grade DCIS. Autopsy prevalence may be inflated by ADH read as DCIS. Recurrence after excision reflects margins and residual disease, **not untreated natural history**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors conclude DCIS is a precursor of most invasive breast cancer but **not all DCIS progresses** in the medium term. Kopans' model shows a large autopsy reservoir is expected even if all DCIS progresses, so reservoir size alone does not establish overdiagnosis.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents DCIS natural history inferred largely from low-grade, biopsy-only lesions. Does not represent high-grade DCIS or contemporary cohorts treated to modern margin standards.

studies.interpretation:
For a radiation oncologist the useful part of this review is less the progression range than how it frames what local therapy is preventing. The direct-observation series, DCIS read as benign and left with biopsy alone, are the only human data on untreated lesions, and they bound progression at 14–53% over a decade or more. The range is wide for structural reasons the authors lay out: the series are small, retrospective, drawn from old pathology archives, and dominated by low-grade lesions because high-grade DCIS was less likely to be misread as benign. Follow-up was incomplete in the highest estimate, where Rosen had outcomes on 15 of 30 women and ascertainment plausibly favoured those who later presented with invasive disease. The range therefore says little about high-grade DCIS, which is the lesion most RT decisions now turn on.

The recurrence data sit closer to practice. In the Boyages meta-analysis, adding RT to conservative surgery lowered overall recurrence from 22.5% to 8.9%, and the gap was widest in comedo-type and necrotic lesions, where CS alone carried 34.4% and 24.7%. Because about half of recurrences after local therapy are invasive, the RT effect on ipsilateral events translates partly into invasive events prevented. The authors are right that recurrence after excision is not natural history: it is conditioned on margins and on what residual disease surgery left, so these numbers describe treated DCIS, not the untreated lesion.

The autopsy reservoir, median 8.9% DCIS against 1.3% occult invasive cancer, is often cited as evidence of overdiagnosis. The review undercuts that reading. Kopans' simple growth model predicts a reservoir up to 20 times the detected number even if every lesion eventually invades, because slow linear growth along ducts keeps many lesions below the detection threshold for years. A large reservoir is compatible with universal progression and cannot by itself justify omitting treatment.

The detail that matters most for de-escalation is latency. Low-grade DCIS recurs less often in short series, but its recurrence rate keeps rising with long follow-up, and in Page's untreated cohort invasive cancers emerged at 23 and 31 years. Any omission argument for low-grade disease built on short-horizon ipsilateral event rates is measuring an incomplete curve. Later work, RTOG 9804 on RT omission and the LORIS, COMET and LORD surveillance trials, are the prospective tests of the question this review could only frame.

What would make the conclusion wrong is mainly misclassification and selection: autopsy prevalence inflated by ADH read as DCIS, and misdiagnosis series inflated by selective follow-up or deflated by their low-grade skew. These biases pull in opposite directions, which is why the authors decline to give a point estimate. For a 2005 synthesis that restraint holds up; the field still lacks a grade-specific progression rate for untreated DCIS.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Low-grade DCIS recurs with longer latency, and Page's untreated cases invaded at 23 and 31 yrs, so short-follow-up omission data undercount late events. The RT reduction in the Boyages pooling held in comedo and necrotic subgroups, where CS alone recurrence was highest.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Recurrence after excision is margin-dependent; mastectomy carried 1.4% recurrence vs 22.5% after CS alone in the Boyages pooling. About half of post-excision recurrences are invasive, which keeps complete excision central even for lesions that might never progress.

studies.name: APBI-IMRT-Florence Technique Update (IMRT to VMAT)
studies.tldr: 30 Gy/5 consecutive-fraction VMAT PBI in 50 pts: no grade >1 acute or late toxicity at median 4.5y; cosmesis excellent/good 98%.
details: 🔍 Single-center series of 50 consecutive pts (39 left, 11 right), all planned and treated free breathing
🔍 Delivery moved from 5-field 6-MV step-and-shoot IMRT to patient-specific partial-arc VMAT
🔍 Schedule moved from every-other-day to consecutive daily 30 Gy/5 fx

details.text: 🔍 Volume definitions updated (authors: formal change only, no actual change in treated volume)
subdetails: Original: CTV = clips + 1 cm, PTV = CTV + 1 cm
Current: CTV = clips + 1.5 cm, PTV = CTV + 0.5 cm
PTV may extend ≤4 mm into ipsilateral lung, cropped 3 mm inside skin

details.text: 🔍 Dose constraints, original protocol vs updated (Table 1); failing the accepted tier → WBI

details: 📐 Ipsilateral breast V15Gy correlates with PTV/ipsilateral breast volume ratio, R2 0.911

subdetails: Dermatitis 28%
Fatigue 4%
Edema 2%, breast pain 2%
Fibrosis 14%
Telangiectasia 2%

details: 📊 Physician-assessed cosmesis (Harvard 4-point): excellent 84%, good 14%, fair 2%

details.text: 🔗 Any-grade toxicity: consecutive-day series vs parent trial (every other day)

details: 🔗 Parent phase 3: no significant IBTR or survival difference vs WBI at 10y; toxicity and cosmesis favored PBI
⚠️ No IBTR or local control reported for the consecutive-day series
⚠️ Follow-up range 0.6-5y (mean 3.4), short for late fibrosis and cosmesis
⚠️ Requires inverse planning; authors flag access gaps and US insurance authorization barriers for IMRT/VMAT

verdict.rationale: Single-center 50-pt series with no comparator; daily schedule departs from the alternate-day phase 3, and no recurrence data are reported for it.
verdict.audience: Low-risk early breast cancer, postoperative PBI candidates

studies.significance: The usable detail is the planning screen: ipsilateral breast V15Gy tracks the PTV/ipsilateral breast volume ratio (R2 0.911), so a high ratio flags a pt likely to fail the V15Gy constraint before optimization. Constraints now carry ideal and accepted tiers, and failing the accepted tier sends the pt to WBI.
studies.monday_clinic: In a low-risk early breast cancer pt planned for PBI with VMAT, this supports the Florence 30 Gy/5 fx schedule on consecutive days from a toxicity standpoint; it does not address 3D-CRT delivery.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-center technical update with a dosimetric and toxicity analysis of **50 consecutive pts** treated on consecutive days (39 left, 11 right), free breathing. Median follow-up **4.5 years** (mean 3.4; range 0.6-5).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **30 Gy in 5 consecutive daily fractions** via patient-specific partial-arc VMAT, replacing the trial's 5-field step-and-shoot IMRT given every other day. CTV = clips + 1.5 cm, PTV = CTV + 0.5 cm, cropped 3 mm from skin and ≤4 mm into lung. If at least the accepted constraints cannot be met, the pt is moved to **WBI**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Mean ipsilateral breast 731 cm3 and mean PTV 139 cm3. Ipsilateral breast V15Gy tracks the PTV/breast volume ratio (**R2 0.911**), so the ratio works as a pre-planning screen for the V15Gy constraint.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute G1 32% and late G1 16%, with **no grade >1** event. Physician-rated cosmesis excellent or good in **98%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The parent APBI-IMRT-Florence phase 3 showed no significant IBTR or survival difference vs WBI at 10 years, with less toxicity. FAST-Forward made 26 Gy/5 fx WBI noninferior to 40 Gy/15 fx, but that schedule has not been tested in a PBI phase 3. Toxicity in this series runs numerically above the trial's every-other-day rates, all grade 1.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents low-risk early breast cancer PBI candidates planned with inverse-planned VMAT at free breathing. Does not represent centers limited to 3D-CRT, prone setups, or pts whose PTV/breast volume ratio fails the V15Gy constraint.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: No IBTR or local control is reported for the consecutive-day series, so efficacy of the schedule change rests on the alternate-day trial. Follow-up starts at 0.6 years, short for late fibrosis and cosmesis.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Daily delivery trades a **numerically higher grade 1 rate** for a 1-week course. The authors cite prone 5-fx data (Shah et al) with 68% treated on consecutive days. Whether consecutive scheduling holds IBTR at trial levels remains open.

studies.interpretation:
A radiation oncologist reading this paper is not asking whether 30 Gy in 5 fractions to the partial breast works. The parent APBI-IMRT-Florence phase 3 already reported no significant difference from WBI in ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence or survival at 10 years, with toxicity and cosmesis favoring PBI. The real question is whether the Florence regimen survives two changes most departments would make on adoption: VMAT in place of multifield step-and-shoot IMRT, and daily rather than alternate-day delivery. This report answers the toxicity half of that question in 50 consecutive pts and says nothing about the efficacy half.

On toxicity the read is reassuring but not neutral. Every event was grade 1, and physician-rated cosmesis was excellent or good in 98%. Both acute and early late grade 1 rates still sit above the trial's alternate-day experience, and the authors acknowledge the direction. With 50 pts the gap could be noise, case mix, or scoring drift between eras. It could also be the expected cost of compressing five fractions into one week. A reader should treat it as an unresolved signal rather than dismiss it because the grades are low. Late fibrosis keeps evolving beyond the follow-up much of this cohort has, and the range begins under one year.

The FAST-Forward context the authors cite cuts both ways. Five-fraction whole breast RT has 5-year normal tissue data, and moderate or marked effects rose at 27 Gy relative to 40 Gy in 15 fractions, showing that dose per fraction in a one-week course has a cost. The Florence regimen gives its 30 Gy in 5 fractions to a much smaller volume, which is the usual argument for why PBI tolerates the schedule, but this series is too small to test that argument directly.

The most transferable content is the planning framework rather than the outcomes. The updated constraint set separates ideal targets from accepted deviations and makes failure of the accepted tier a trigger to switch to WBI, which gives a new program a defensible exit rule. The near-linear relation between ipsilateral breast V15Gy and the PTV to breast volume ratio lets a planner screen candidates before optimization; the authors note the relation breaks down for ratios above 50%, where the constraint itself caps V15Gy. The margin redesign (larger CTV expansion, smaller PTV expansion) is described as formal, so the treated volume should be comparable to the trial's.

What would make daily-schedule adoption wrong is an excess of ipsilateral recurrence or late fibrosis that this cohort cannot detect. Until a larger daily-schedule series reports recurrence with longer follow-up, the defensible position is that the trial's efficacy evidence belongs to the alternate-day schedule, and the daily version has a plausible but unproven claim to it. The authors also flag that inverse-planned delivery is not universally available or reimbursed. The planning comparison they cite suggests 3D-CRT can meet acceptable target coverage and organ doses with some loss of homogeneity and conformity, which matters for centers that cannot use VMAT.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Ipsilateral breast V15Gy tracks the PTV/ipsilateral breast volume ratio (R2 0.911), giving a pre-planning screen for the V15Gy constraint. The updated constraints add an accepted-deviation tier, and failing it routes the pt to WBI, which gives a clear exit rule for adopting the daily 30 Gy/5 fx schedule.

open_questions: IBTR with consecutive vs alternate-day 30 Gy/5 fx PBI
Late fibrosis and cosmesis beyond 5 years with daily delivery
Can 3D-CRT meet the updated Florence constraints?

studies.name: Implications of Genetic Testing on RT Decisions: A Guide for Radiation Oncologists
studies.tldr: ASTRO think tank: heterozygous germline variants (BRCA1/2, PALB2, CHEK2, VUS) should not alter indicated RT; deleterious ATM in young pts is the exception.
details: 🔍 ASTRO-convened think tank (February 2019): genetics, genomics, radiosensitivity, risk-estimate and clinical oncology experts

details.text: 🔍 Consensus RT read by variant class

rows: No increased RT toxicity or RT-induced second cancer with standard adjuvant RT
Should not affect RT decisions (extended from BRCA data)
Avoid optional RT, esp. young pts; close CBC screening after indicated RT
No known excess acute/late toxicity; in-field second malignancy risk thought elevated
Avoid RT; RT for MPNST considered if margin-negative resection not achievable

details: 📊 ATM missense/truncating carriers: 5-yr CBC risk 2.9% → 3.8% (RR 1.3, EAR 0.9%), worked example
⚠️ ATM toxicity data evenly split: as much evidence of no excess risk as of modest excess risk
📐 ATM rs1801516 SNP (~24% of 5456 breast/prostate pts): acute toxicity OR 1.5, late OR 1.2; not deemed actionable
📊 Hereditary retinoblastoma: EBRT → 30-yr second cancer incidence 35% vs 6% without RT
📊 Somatic ATM truncation: better radiographic local control after palliative RT vs ATM VUS/wildtype (P < .001); OS no different

subdetails: 9% developed a second solid malignancy at mean 12-yr f/u
~8% of second cancers attributed to RT
EAR of RT-attributable second solid malignancy 0.5% by 15 yr

details: ⚠️ Many cited series lack a no-RT control, so predictive vs prognostic effects can't be separated
studies.significance: The ATM carve-out rests on small absolute numbers: a carrier's 5-yr contralateral breast cancer risk moves from 2.9% to 3.8% (EAR 0.9%), and toxicity data are evenly split. Somatic ATM truncation points the other way, with better local control after palliative RT (P < .001), which is the case for genomically adjusted dose rather than omission.
studies.monday_clinic: In a young pt with a deleterious heterozygous ATM mutation weighing optional RT, this supports deferral or close CBC screening after indicated RT; it does not extend to BRCA1/2, PALB2, CHEK2 or VUS carriers, whose indicated RT is unchanged.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **ASTRO think tank** convened February 2019; expert consensus across genetic screening, radiosensitivity, risk estimation and clinical oncology. Emphasis on the **excess risk conferred by RT** above a variant's background risk.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **VUS = normal.** **BRCA1/2, PALB2, CHEK2, RAD50/51 should not change RT decisions.** **Deleterious heterozygous ATM**: avoid optional RT in young pts, screen for CBC after indicated RT.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: BRCA reassurance aligns with NCCN counseling guidance and multiple adjuvant RT series. The PALB2/CHEK2 extension is by **phenotypic analogy** to BRCA, not carrier-specific RT outcome data.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with heterozygous germline variants found on screening or paired tumor-normal sequencing. Does not represent rare radiosensitivity syndromes such as ataxia telangiectasia or Li-Fraumeni, which carry their own risks.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Candidate SNP findings often failed replication; low mutation frequency limits even large cohorts. Current registries lack **dose distribution** and prospective toxicity grading needed to validate variants.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Actionable toxicity prediction is expected to be **polygenic**, not single-gene. Future genomically guided RT trials should include a **no-RT arm** to separate prognostic from predictive value.

studies.interpretation:
The document's value is that it turns a recurring clinic anxiety into a default: a heterozygous germline DNA-repair variant is not, by itself, a reason to modify or withhold indicated RT. That default is strongest where the data are strongest. For BRCA1/2 the panel describes fairly consistent clinical data showing no excess toxicity or RT-induced second cancer with standard adjuvant regimens, and it sits comfortably beside NCCN counseling guidance for those carriers. The extension to PALB2, CHEK2 and RAD50/51 is weaker in kind. It is an argument by phenotypic analogy from BRCA, not a body of carrier-specific RT outcome data, and a reader should hold it with that in mind.

ATM is where the consensus applies caution, and also where it is least certain. The panel states that the evidence for and against excess toxicity in heterozygous carriers is evenly balanced, so the advice to defer optional RT in young carriers is driven mainly by the second-cancer question. Even there, the worked contralateral breast example (5-yr risk 2.9% to 3.8%, EAR 0.9%) frames the stake as small in absolute terms, which is why the same document says indicated RT still outweighs it. The decision that moves is narrow: optional RT, where omission is a reasonable alternative, not adjuvant RT with a clear benefit.

Methodologically this is expert consensus from a single convened meeting, built on observational series, candidate-gene and SNP studies, and preclinical work. Many underlying studies lack an unirradiated control group, which the authors flag as the reason predictive and prognostic effects cannot be separated. Candidate SNP findings have often failed replication; the ATM rs1801516 association is the exception with meta-analytic support, yet its odds ratios (1.5 acute, 1.2 late) are modest and not considered actionable. Low mutation frequency means even large cohorts will struggle to reach definitive conclusions for any single variant.

The forward argument is that single-gene screening is the wrong unit. The panel expects actionable prediction to come from polygenic scores built in prospective resources such as REQUITE and the Radiogenomics Consortium, with dose distribution and prospective toxicity grading linked to genotype. The somatic ATM signal (better local control after palliative RT with truncating mutations, OS unchanged) points the other way: the same repair defect that might raise normal tissue risk may raise tumor sensitivity, which is the rationale for genomically adjusted dose trials that include a no-RT arm.

What would make this wrong is a carrier-specific dataset showing clinically meaningful excess late toxicity or in-field malignancy in PALB2 or CHEK2 carriers; the reassurance there is inferential. This is a 2019 position, so a reader applying it should check whether later data have narrowed the ATM uncertainty.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The ATM carve-out rests on small absolute numbers: 5-yr contralateral breast cancer risk 2.9% to 3.8% (EAR 0.9%), with toxicity data evenly split. Somatic ATM truncation instead predicted better local control after palliative RT (P < .001), favoring dose individualization over omission.

Genomically adjusted RT dose vs standard protocol
